4.text: Chukchee incantations mention another “giant fish,” called Kañaˊolhɪn.

5.text: The name is used to designate sculpin; but the giant Kañaˊyolhɪn has existed

6.text: as a separate fish from “the first limit of creation.” It lies motionless in the

7.text: middle of the sea. Its body has become an island, and moss grows on its

8.text: back. The latter details have a marked resemblance to the description of a

9.text: fabulous whale in the nursery tales of the Old World.

10.text: Vaˊamên is a kind of triton which exists apparently somewhere in the

11.text: waters of northeastern Siberia, on the Arctic or on the Pacific shore, though

26.text: The “mountain echo” (ᴇˊnmɪ-taˊañ) lives in the open, among the mountains.

27.text: Its body is of stone, and its mouth and eyes are located on its breast. The

28.text: “mountain echo” is also described as a young, pretty woman wandering about

29.text: among the rocks. In one tale, she marries a man, but, on account of jealousy,

30.text: is killed by his former wife.² The “echo of the wood” (ɵˊttɪ-taˊañ) lives in the

31.text: poplar-forest. It has a wooden body, without hands or feet, and resembles

32.text: the old trunk of a tree.

33.text: The “black bear” is a wife who was forsaken by her husband for an-

34.text: other woman. She revenged herself by killing him and her rival.² The

35.text: “mountain sheep” is also a woman forsaken by her husband. She threw

36.text: herself from a steep rock, and was dashed against the stones, thus becoming

37.text: a sheep. Her braided hair was turned into horns.

38.text: The “black beetle,” called in Chukchee Täˊqɪ-ñeˊut (the name means literally

39.text: “shining black woman”), affords a third story of an unfortunate wife. When

40.text: her husband forsook her, she killed him by pouring into his ear water taken

41.text: from a piece of old sea-ice. According to one tale, the “black beetle” over-
